sources.fact: As the body goes through puberty, the larynx grows larger and thicker and the vocal cords grow longer and thicker. As a boy's body adjusts to this changing equipment, his voice may crack or break. The bump at the front of the throat is the Adam's apple, formed as the larynx angles differently. Girls' voices only deepen by a couple of tones and the change is barely noticeable. This process lasts only a few months.

Before puberty the larynx sits higher in the neck; in puberty it enlarges and moves lower, and the vocal folds thicken and enlarge. Boys' voices can suddenly drop about an octave lower; girls' pitch drops only about three tones.

math.note: about one octave drop for boys (Cleveland Clinic)
about three tones drop for girls (Cleveland Clinic); KidsHealth says 'a couple of tones'

Puberty can drop a boy's voice by about an octave. Sometimes it trips on the way down 🎸

During puberty the larynx (voice box) grows and moves lower, and the vocal cords get longer and thicker. While the body gets used to the new equipment, the voice can crack. Girls' voices drop too, but only by about three tones.

The cracking usually lasts only a few months: your voice isn't broken, it's being upgraded.
